title: Signature Alive-State Boot
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature alive-state boot is an original design in which the boot sequence carries a small liveness record from the first sector onward: each boot stage writes a short state note, including its stage number and a checksum, into a reserved area before handing control to the next stage. If a later stage fails, the notes show exactly how far booting got, which turns a silent hang into a diagnosable stop. The design is presented as a design, not as a shipped bootloader.

Alive-state notes are deliberately tiny, because boot stages run with almost no services available. A stage number, a checksum, and a status code fit in a handful of bytes and can be written with the same simple output the stage already uses. The reserved area is cleared only after a successful boot, so a failed boot leaves its trail intact for the next attempt to read and report.

The demo simulates four boot stages writing their notes in turn and then prints the trail, including a checksum check per stage. It is a design simulation in ordinary Python, not a bootloader, and it claims no hardware behavior.

title: Signature Hardened Flat Binary
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature hardened flat binary is an original design that adds a small verified header to the flat-binary idea: a magic number, an entry offset, a segment table, and a header checksum that the loader verifies before copying anything. The header is deliberately smaller than a full executable format, because the goal is a minimal system whose loader can be read and audited in one sitting, while still refusing files that fail their own checksum.

Hardening here means refusal, not cleverness: a bad magic, a segment that runs past the declared image size, or a checksum mismatch all stop the load with a plain error instead of jumping into suspect bytes. The loader also zeroes the gap between segments, so stale bytes from a previous program cannot leak into the new one. Those rules are easy to state and easy to test, which is the point.

The demo builds a header and two segments, verifies magic, bounds, and checksum, and prints the load plan. It loads into a Python dictionary, not machine memory, and it is a design exercise rather than a shipped loader.

title: Signature Identity-Seeded Kernel
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature identity-seeded kernel is an original design in which a small identity seed, derived from the machine's own boot record, seeds the kernel's deterministic choices: the order of early self-tests, the layout of its first tables, and the pattern of its first log lines. The seed changes nothing about correctness, because every seeded choice is one of several equally valid orders, but it makes each machine's boot trace distinguishable, which helps tell two identical-looking boots apart in logs.

Seeding is kept out of security decisions on purpose: the seed is not a secret, not a key, and not an authentication factor, and no access decision in the design depends on it. Its only job is determinism with variety, so that a repeated boot on the same machine reproduces the same trace, while a different machine's trace differs in exactly the seeded places. That property is what makes the seed useful for diagnosis rather than for trust.

The demo derives a small seed from a boot string, shuffles the self-test order deterministically from it, and prints the order twice to show it reproduces. It is a design simulation, not a kernel, and it claims no security property.

Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. The Signature Quad-Helix file explorer is an original design for browsing a small archive through four linked views, called strands, that always show the same collection from different angles: by name, by kind, by ladder tier, and by most recent change. Moving the cursor in one strand moves the focus in the others, so the user never loses their place when switching views. The design targets tiny archives that fit comfortably in memory, not general filesystems.

Each strand is a sorted list over the same records, and the explorer keeps one focus record shared across all four. A search narrows all strands at once, and clearing the search restores them, which keeps the interaction model to two operations: move and filter. The design document stresses that the explorer shows records, never rewrites them, so browsing cannot corrupt the archive it displays.

The demo builds four strands over eight records, focuses one record, and prints its position in each strand. It is a design prototype in Python, not a shipped file manager.

The Signature archive engine is an original design for a small record store with three rules: records are never edited in place, every record carries its own identifier and ladder tier, and a search scans titles, bodies, and identifiers together. Appending a corrected record supersedes the old one without erasing it, so the archive keeps its own history and a reader can always see what changed and when.

title: Signature Deterministic OS Layer
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature deterministic OS layer is an original design for a small operating layer whose observable behavior depends only on its inputs and its seed, never on wall-clock timing or on the order in which outside events happen to arrive. Inputs are queued, processed in a fixed order, and logged, so the same input sequence always produces the same output sequence. That property makes the layer testable in a way that timing-dependent systems are not.

Determinism is enforced by three rules: no direct reads of the clock inside decision code, no unseeded randomness, and no processing order that depends on arrival timing. Anything that needs the time receives it as an explicit input value, and anything that needs randomness receives it from the seeded generator. The design is explicit that determinism aids testing and diagnosis; it does not by itself make the system correct or secure.

The demo feeds the same input sequence twice through a tiny deterministic layer and prints both outputs to show they match exactly. It is a design simulation, not an operating system.

title: Signature Identity Context Switch
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature identity context switch is an original design for cooperative switching in which each task carries a short identity tag, and the scheduler logs the outgoing tag, the incoming tag, and a step count at every switch. The log is the point: when a small system misbehaves, the switch log shows exactly which task ran, in which order, and for how long, without needing any external debugger.

The switch itself follows the cooperative pattern: a task yields, the scheduler saves its continuation, picks the next ready task, and resumes it. The identity tags add no privilege and no access control; they are labels for the log, and the design says so plainly so that nobody mistakes a label for a security boundary. A task that never yields still starves the system, and the design does not pretend otherwise.

The demo runs two tagged tasks through a cooperative loop, logs each switch, and prints the log. It is a design prototype in Python, not a real thread implementation.

title: Signature IDT and TSS Design
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature IDT and TSS design is an original design for interrupt handling in a tiny protected-mode kernel: an interrupt descriptor table with one gate per vector the kernel actually serves, plus a task state segment that gives each privilege transition a known stack. The table is built from a short list of vector-to-handler pairs, and any vector not in the list has no gate, so an unexpected interrupt faults loudly instead of running an unintended handler.

The task state segment exists in this design for one job only: supplying a stack when the processor changes privilege level. The kernel does not use hardware task switching, because that mechanism is complex and unnecessary at this scale; it uses the segment as a stack table and performs switching in software. Keeping the segment's role narrow keeps the design auditable.

The demo builds a gate list from six vector-handler pairs, checks that every gate has a handler name, and prints the table. It models table construction, not real descriptor hardware.

title: Signature Syscall ABI
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature syscall ABI is an original design for a tiny call table with stable numbers: each number names one operation, each operation documents its arguments and its return values, and numbers are never reused for a different operation. The first version of the table carries only the calls a minimal system needs: write, read, exit, identity, and time as an explicit input value rather than a clock read.

Stability is the ABI's main promise, and the design protects it with a rule: adding a call appends a new number, and changing a call's behavior ships under a new number while the old number keeps its old behavior. That rule costs table space and saves programs, which is the right trade for a system whose users build long-lived tools on top of it.

The demo dispatches the five documented calls plus one unknown number, printing each result and the unknown-number error. It models dispatch logic, not a real trap.

title: Signature Compression Component
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature compression component is an original design for a small archive compressor built from two ideas: a dictionary pass that replaces repeated phrases with short references, and a run-length pass for long repeats of a single byte. The component is designed for the archive engine's records, which repeat headings and field names often, so dictionary matches are common and the compressed size falls noticeably on real archive text.

The component stores its dictionary beside the data and verifies every decompression by comparing a checksum of the restored bytes with the checksum recorded at compression time. A mismatch reports corruption instead of returning damaged text, because an archive that silently returns wrong records is worse than an archive that reports a bad one. The design is explicit that this is a teaching compressor, not a competitor to production formats.

The demo compresses a short repeated phrase with run-length encoding, decompresses it, and checks that the round trip restores the original exactly. It demonstrates the round-trip rule, not a full compressor.

title: Signature Boot Chain
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature boot chain is an original design linking the alive-state boot stages into one verifiable sequence: each stage checks the previous stage's note before running, and writes its own note before passing control onward. A stage that finds a missing or corrupt note stops with a plain error naming the stage it expected, instead of running on top of an unknown state. The chain turns boot order from an assumption into a checked sequence.

Each note carries the stage number, a short name, and a checksum over the note's own fields, so a note can be validated without trusting the stage that wrote it. The final stage reports the whole chain, which gives a failed boot a readable history and a successful boot a short receipt. The design keeps notes small because early stages cannot afford large structures.

The demo simulates a five-stage chain, verifies each note in turn, and prints the chain with its verification result. It is a design simulation, not a bootloader.

title: Signature Memory Guard
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature memory guard is an original design for a tiny allocator that fences every allocation with guard values: a known pattern written just before and just after each block, checked on every free and on every allocation sweep. A write that runs past its block corrupts a guard first, and the next check reports the corruption with the block's identity instead of letting the damage surface later as an unrelated crash.

Guards catch overflows; they do not prevent them, and the design says so. Prevention would need hardware bounds or a language-level guarantee, neither of which a tiny C-style kernel has by default. The guard's value is diagnosis: it turns silent corruption into a named failure at the next check, which is often close enough in time to find the offending code.

The demo allocates two guarded blocks, corrupts one guard deliberately, runs a sweep, and prints which block failed its guard check. It is a design prototype, not a production allocator.

title: Signature Tick Heartbeat
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature tick heartbeat is an original design for a tiny scheduler heartbeat: every tick, the kernel advances a counter, runs due events, and writes one heartbeat line containing the tick number, the number of events run, and a running checksum of the event names. The heartbeat is both a clock and a log, so a stalled system shows a frozen heartbeat and a runaway system shows a heartbeat full of unexpected events.

Heartbeat lines are written to the same console the shell uses, but they are prefixed so they can be filtered out of ordinary output. The design keeps the heartbeat cheap: one line per tick, no allocation, and a checksum computed by addition rather than by any cryptographic function, because the heartbeat is a diagnostic aid and not a security log.

The demo runs ten ticks with events on three of them, prints the heartbeat lines, and verifies the final checksum by recomputation. It is a design simulation, not a timer interrupt handler.

title: Signature Console Bridge
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature console bridge is an original design for joining the kernel console to the shell without letting either side block the other: input arrives into a small ring buffer, the shell drains it when it is ready, and output goes through a second ring buffer that the console drains at its own pace. If either buffer fills, the writer drops the oldest line and counts the drop, so a flood degrades into a counted loss instead of a deadlock.

Ring buffers suit this job because they are fixed-size, allocation-free, and easy to reason about: a head index, a tail index, and a rule for full versus empty. The bridge adds one rule of its own, which is that control lines, such as the heartbeat prefix, are never dropped in favor of ordinary output, so diagnostics survive exactly when the system is busiest.

The demo feeds twelve lines through a four-slot ring, counts the drops, and prints the surviving lines in order. It is a design prototype, not a real console driver.

title: Signature Alive-State Snapshot

The Signature alive-state snapshot is an original design for capturing a tiny system's state at a chosen moment: the register-like values the design tracks, the ready queue, the tick counter, and the console buffer's tail, all copied into a snapshot record with a checksum. A later snapshot can be compared field by field with the earlier one, which makes it possible to say exactly what changed between two moments instead of guessing from logs.

Snapshots are read-only records; restoring one is a separate, deliberate operation that the design treats as a restart with known state, not as a time-travel trick. The design notes that a snapshot of a tiny system is small enough to print in full, and it recommends printing it, because a state record nobody reads is only a ritual.

The demo builds two snapshots of a small state, diffs them field by field, and prints the changed fields. It is a design prototype, not a checkpointing system.

title: Signature Combo PC Integration
body:
Signature design: this record describes an original design in the Signature edition. It is labeled Signature throughout and is never presented as an established public fact or as a working product. Its feasibility tier states plainly how far the design has been carried: buildable-now, research-stage, or speculative.

The Signature Combo PC integration is an original design for joining the pair's pieces into one minimal system: the alive-state boot chain starts the identity-seeded kernel, the kernel runs the deterministic layer, the archive engine and file explorer sit above the syscall ABI, and the compression component serves the archive. Each piece keeps its own interface, so any piece can be tested alone before the whole is assembled, and the integration document lists the assembly order explicitly.

Integration is where small designs usually fail, because interfaces that looked compatible on paper disagree about details like who owns a buffer or who reports an error. The design answers those questions in advance: the caller owns buffers, the callee reports errors by return value, and no piece allocates during another piece's critical section. Those three rules are the whole integration contract, and the design treats breaking one as breaking the system.

The demo assembles the pieces in order, checks each interface name against the contract list, and prints the assembled system with its piece count. It is a design checklist in Python, not a booting system, and it claims no working machine.
